title: Rationalize embed & reranker pagination stability for legacy clients
creator: Ava Martinez
description:
Background:
Many customers run older SDKs and partner integrations that expect stable pagination cursors and deterministic HTTP mapping from embeddings and rerank endpoints. Recent runtime changes (streaming previews, structured outputs, and a small HTTP error normalization) exposed minor incompatibilities: transient 503 vs 429 surface, cursor format changes when we switched to cursor-prefetching, and slightly different page-size semantics between /embeddings/search and /rerank/score.

Goal:
- Provide a minimal compatibility layer that preserves existing cursor semantics and HTTP error mappings for legacy clients while allowing runtime improvements for newer clients.
- Make the contract explicit in docs and add a migration guide.

Scope (what we will do):
- Add a compat flag in the API surface: accept header x-redwood-compat: "embed-v1" or query param ?compat=embed-v1 to trigger legacy behaviors for a request token.
- Normalize pagination cursors for legacy mode: length-prefixed base64 signature identical to historical implementation (no prefetch KV encoding).
- Map transient backend throttling to the historical HTTP status codes for legacy mode (e.g., 429 when client quota exceeded, 503 only for infra-level outages).
- Provide canonical examples and a short migration script in SDKs.

Out of scope:
- Rewriting server-side KV cache logic to always preserve old cursor format for all requests. New clients will use new cursor format by default.
- Full compatibility for non-embeddings endpoints (other compatibility efforts will be tracked separately).

Acceptance criteria:
- Legacy-mode requests from existing SDKs (integration test matrix) receive identical cursor strings and HTTP codes as in production snapshot 2025-11-01 for a representative sample of queries.
- No measurable regression in throughput/latency for normal requests (<= 3% tail increase).
- Documentation and SDK changelogs and migration guide published before release.

Design notes and trade-offs:
- Option A: Autosense client by user-agent vs explicit compat header. Autosense is convenient but risks false positives; we prefer explicit flag and SDK updates to set it.
- Option B: Keep both cursor formats and make runtime decode-aware. Chosen: store a format-version marker in new cursors; compat flow generates old-style cursors and decoders accept both. This costs small extra codepath but isolates legacy behavior.

Implementation plan (high level):
1) API layer: accept compat param and route to compat normalization middleware (ENG work).
2) Runtime: add generator for legacy cursor strings in compat mode and a decoder that accepts both formats (ENG + infra).
3) Error mapping: small error-remap table in API gateway for compat mode (ENG).
4) Integration tests: build replay tests against a snapshot to assert cursor equality and http codes (QA + ENG).
5) SDKs: add compat header helper and migration snippet to node/python SDKs (DX + SDK).
6) Docs: migration guide, examples, and deprecation timeline (PM + DX).

Testing & rollout:
- Canary rollout to 5% traffic for compat header requests only. Monitor: cursor-parity success, error-rate delta, latency P95.
- If instability observed, we will roll back compat header or throttle via request sampling.

Monitoring signals and dashboards:
- New dashboard: compat-mode request ratio, parity-failures (tests asserting cursor mismatch), HTTP-mapping-delta, customer-errors (support tickets tagged 'cursor').

Risks and mitigations:
- Risk: inadvertent acceptance of compat header by intermediate proxies. Mitigation: require both header and SDK token scope to enable compat (API gateway check).
- Risk: increased code complexity leading to subtle bugs. Mitigation: pair ENG reviewers for critical path, add end-to-end parity tests.
